Up to the $x$ free tax the $x$–relevant part of the expected payment is

$$
{\cal C}_{0}(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta)
           =(1-\theta )F(\theta )\,h(x),\qquad h(x):=xp(x),
$$

and with the normalisation $C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta )$
$$

      =p(1)h(\theta ),\qquad 
h(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0\; {\rm  on\;}(0,1) .
$$
For $0\le\theta<1$

$$
h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<-F(\theta)<0 ,
$$

because $F>0,\;F'\le 0$, so that $h(\theta)$ and hence $\Delta(\theta)$
is strictly decreasing on the admissible interval and

$$
\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad \Delta(1)=0 .
$$

Hence on the interior

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=C(\theta ,1),
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$
i.e. up to the $x$ independent term $t(\theta)$
$$
\operatorname*{argmin}_{x}C(\theta ,x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x}h(x),
\qquad \theta<1,
$$
so that for the usual $h'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)>0$ we have the unique
interior best reply

$$
x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,\qquad 
C(1,x)\equiv t(1),
$$

and $x^{*}(1)$ is undetermined.  In particular

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
 =h'(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]<0 ,\qquad \theta<1,
$$

so $C(\theta ,x)$ is submodular in $(\theta ,x)$ and $x^{*}(\theta)$
is weakly increasing in $\theta$.  The extra expected penalty of a
strict auditor relative to the lenient one is
$\Delta(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$, it is strictly decreasing in
truthfulness and it vanishes only in the limit $(1-\theta)F(\theta)\to0$.

In the strict single-crossing sense

$$
\frac{d}{d\theta}\Delta(\theta)>0\iff h'(\theta)>0
\iff (1-\theta)F'(\theta)>F(\theta)
\iff -F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0 ,
$$

which is impossible on $0\le\theta\le1$; formally $h'>0$ would require
$1-\theta<0$, i.e. $\theta>1$ outside the admissible domain.  Hence in
the strict monotone sense the set

$$
\{\theta: x^{*}(\theta')<x^{*}(\theta)\ {\rm for\ }\theta'>\theta\}
\subset[0,1]
$$

is empty.  Weakly $x=0$ weakly dominates $x=1$ for every admissible
$\theta\le1$ and strictly dominates it for every $\theta<1$.  On the
binary support $\theta\in\{0,1\}$ this is

* $\theta=0$ : $C(0,0)=t(0)<t(0)+p(1)F(0)=C(0,1)$, the malpractice
type strictly prefers the lenient auditor $x^{*}(0)=0$;
* $\theta=1$ : $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$, the truthful type is indifferent,

boundary $\theta=1$.  This is the familiar perverse, essentially
empty, sorting: the incentive to avoid a strict auditor,
$(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$, is maximal for the malpractice type and
is eroded monotonically to zero as $\theta\uparrow1$, i.e. more
truthful firms are weakly more willing to use the strict, reputable
auditor. ∎

$$

       =(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=p(1)h(\theta),\qquad

$$

$$
h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<-F(\theta)<0,
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

because $F'\le 0$.  Hence $h$ and $\Delta$ are strictly decreasing on
$[0,1)$ and

$$
\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad \Delta(1)=0 .
$$

$$
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\iff(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,
$$

and $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$.  For every interior type the lenient auditor
$x=0$ is the unique minimiser and

$$
x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0\qquad0\le\theta<1,\qquad 
x^{*}(1)\ {\rm indifferent},
$$

i.e. up to the trivial indifference at the top the best response is
constant.  The cross–partial

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
      =h'(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]<0
$$

on the usual $p+xp'>0$ domain, so $C$ is sub-modular in $(\theta ,x)$
and $x^{*}(\theta)$ is weakly increasing in $\theta$.  The incremental
cost of moving from lenient to strict,

$$
\Delta C(\theta;x',x)=\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]h(\theta ),\qquad 
\frac{d}{d\theta}\Delta C<0,
$$

is strictly decreasing in truthfulness: the more truthful the firm the
smaller the expected loss from a refusal and the smaller the premium
for leniency.

$$

strict monotone sense the set

\end{equation*}

$(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$, is strictly decreasing in truthfulness.
Hence

\begin{equation*}
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
 =g'(\theta)\!\left[p(x)+xp'(x)\right]<0
\end{equation*}
on the usual $p+xp'>0$ region and $C(\theta ,x)$ is submodular in
$(\theta ,x)$.  The optimal auditor is therefore weakly increasing in
$\theta$; the incentive to avoid the strict auditor is weaker, not
stronger, the more truthful the firm is.

In strict monotone terms the single crossing condition

\begin{equation*}
\frac{d}{d\theta}\Big[C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)\Big]>0
\iff g'(\theta)>0
\iff -F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0,
\end{equation*}
i.e. $(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>F(\theta)$, can never be satisfied on the
admissible set $0\le\theta\le1$; formally $g'>0$ would require
$1-\theta<0$, i.e. $\theta>1$.  Hence on the economically relevant
domain the strict monotone comparative static $ \theta_{2}>\theta_{1}
\Rightarrow x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$ is empty.  Up to the
trivial indifference at the top of the distribution the lenient auditor
is the unique strict optimum for every imperfectly truthful type,
$\theta<1$, and with the usual tie break $x^{*}\equiv0$ on the whole
support.  On the conventional binary support $\theta\in\{0,1\}$ this is
the strict preference $x^{*}(0)=0$, $C(0,0)=t(0)<t(0)+p(1)F(0)=C(0,1)$,
with $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.  This is the familiar pooling / perverse sorting
result: the more truthful a firm is the smaller the loss from a strict
auditor and the model predicts, weakly, $x^{*}$ increasing, i.e. more
truthful firms being weakly more willing to use the strict, reputable,
auditor.  The weak preference for leniency is $g(\theta)>0$, i.e.
$0\le\theta<1$, and in the binary notation the only strict preference
for leniency is the malpractice type $\theta=0$ with indifference at the
perfectly truthful limit $\theta=1$. ∎

Up to the $x$-independent tax $t(\theta)$ the relevant expected
payment is

$$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta )+x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta ),\qquad x\in\{0,1\},$$

so that for the two admissible auditors

$$C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$$

and

$$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)
      =p(1)h(\theta),\qquad h(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0 .$$

With $F>0$, $F'\le0$,

$$h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<-F(\theta)<0, \qquad0\le\theta<1,$$

so $h$ and hence $\Delta$ is strictly decreasing on the admissible
interval and $\Delta(\theta)\ge0$ with $\Delta(\theta)=0$ iff
$(1-\theta)F(\theta)=0$.  In particular

$$\Delta(\theta)>0\iff (1-\theta)F(\theta)>0\iff \theta<1,$$
$$\Delta(1)=0,$$

i.e. up to the additive $t(\theta)$

$$C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\quad\text{for }\theta<1,\qquad 
C(1,0)=C(1,1).$$

Hence on the interior $(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0$ the lenient auditor $x=0$
strictly dominates the strict auditor.  The excess expected penalty of
using the strict auditor,
$(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$, is the cost advantage of leniency and it is
strictly decreasing in truthfulness, so the incentive to stay with the
lenient auditor is present for every imperfectly truthful type and is
weakened, not strengthened, by an increase in $\theta$.  In the usual
weak order the best reply is therefore

$$x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,$$

with indifference $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$ at the top type $\theta=1$.
On the two point support this is the strict preference for leniency
at the malpractice type $\theta=0$,

$$C(0,0)=t(0)<t(0)+p(1)F(0)=C(0,1),$$

and indifference at the truthful type $\theta=1$.  In the continuous
notation the (weak) region in which the lenient auditor is the unique
best reply, and hence in which an increase in truthfulness is
accompanied by the weakly more lenient best reply $x^{*}\equiv0$,
is $(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0$, i.e. $0\le\theta<1$, and on the stated
discrete support $\theta\in\{0,1\}$ this is the interior type
$\theta=0$ with the conventional limit indifference at $\theta=1$.
Up to the customary tie-break at the top the model therefore predicts
pooling on the lenient auditor for the whole interior of the type
space, the cost advantage $D(\theta)=p(1)h(\theta)$ being strictly
decreasing in $\theta$ and vanishing only at $\theta=1$. ∎

Up to the $x$ independent tax term the relevant ex-ante payment is

$$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta )+x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta ),\qquad 
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta ),$$

so with the two-point audit technology

$$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=(1-\theta )p(1)F(\theta)\ge0,$$

with $p(1)>0$, $F(\theta)>0$.  In particular $C(\theta ,0)\le C(\theta ,1)$
for every admissible $\theta$ and

$$\Delta(\theta)=0\iff (1-\theta)F(\theta)=0\iff\theta=1$$
on the support $0\le\theta\le1$.

Hence for every $\theta<1$ the lenient auditor is strictly cheaper and the
excess expected cost of the strict auditor,
$\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)$, is a product of two weakly
decreasing maps.  $t,p,F$ are only assumed decreasing, not differentiable,
and the problem is set up so that the IFT is not available.  What can be
said without differentiability is therefore only weak monotonicity:
$(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ is weakly decreasing in $\theta$ and so is
$\Delta(\theta)$.  The strict sign of $h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$
used in the usual $h'$-proofs requires $F'$ to exist, which is explicitly
ruled out.  With only monotonicity the comparative static is a weak one:
the weight on the auditor term $g(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ is
weakly decreasing, so

$$C(\theta ,x)-C(\theta ,x') =\big[g(\theta)\big]\big[xp(x)-x'p(x')\big]$$

has decreasing differences in $(\theta ,x)$ and the set of minimisers
$x^{*}(\theta)$ is weakly decreasing in $\theta$ in the Topkis sense.

On the binary lattice this is $x^{*}(\theta)=0$ for every $\theta<1$ and
$C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$.  The strict preference for leniency is therefore
$ \Delta(\theta)>0$, i.e. $0\le\theta<1$, and it weakens as $\theta$ rises
because the refusal risk $1-\theta$ and the penalty $F(\theta)$ both fall.
The only payoff-relevant margin at which the extra cost of strictness is
exhausted is where the refusal term vanishes, $g(\theta)=0$.  On the stated
discrete support this is the top type

$$\Delta(\theta)=0\iff\theta=1,$$

where $(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=0$ and the firm is indifferent between
$x=0$ and $x=1$.  With the conventional tie-break to the cheaper auditor
the indifference is resolved in favour of leniency, i.e. the high-truthfulness
region is the one in which the cost advantage of the strict auditor has
been driven to zero and the firm can be described as choosing the lenient
auditor on the margin.  In the two-point formulation the weak monotone
switch is therefore realised at the perfectly truthful type $\theta=1$,
the limit of the regime $\theta<1$ in which the lenient auditor is the
unique strict optimum.  This is the usual statement of the decreasing
association $x^{*}(\theta)\downarrow$ in the weak order, the degenerate
boundary being the truthful type.

With the $\theta$-free tax term dropped the part of the expected payment which
is $x$ dependent is

$$G(\theta ,x)=(1-\theta )F(\theta )\,h(x),\qquad 
h(x):=x\,p(x)\ge 0,$$

and on the two point lattice

$$C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta), $$

so that up to $t(\theta)$

$$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)
      =(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=p(1)h_{0}(\theta),\qquad 
h_{0}(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,$$
is the excess expected penalty of the strict auditor.  Put
$g(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$.  Then

$$g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<-F(\theta)<0 ,
\qquad 0\le \theta<1, $$

because $F>0$ and $F'\le 0$.  Hence $g$ and $\Delta$ are strictly
decreasing on the admissible interval and

$$\Delta(\theta)>0\iff \theta<1,\qquad \Delta(1)=0,
\qquad 
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\iff\theta<1 .$$

In particular

$$\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
 =\big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big]\,
   \big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]<0   $$
on the usual $p+xp'>0$ region, so $C$ is submodular in $(\theta ,x)$
and $x^{*}(\theta)$ is weakly increasing in $\theta$.  For $\theta<1$

$${\rm argmin}_{x}C(\theta ,x)={\rm argmin}_{x}h(x),$$

i.e. the $\theta$ weight $g(\theta)$ drops out of the first order
condition.  With the binary technology $h(0)=0<h(1)=p(1)$,

$$x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0,\qquad0\le\theta<1, $$
and $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$, so the truthful type is indifferent between
$x=0$ and $x=1$.  The extra cost of going from the lenient to the
strict auditor is

$$\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta),$$

which is strictly decreasing in truthfulness.  The incentive to avoid
the strict auditor is therefore strongest at the malpractice end and is
eroded monotonically with $\theta$, vanishing only at the limit
$g(\theta)=0$.

Hence in the strict monotone sense

$$\frac{d}{d\theta}\Delta(\theta)>0\iff
g'(\theta)>0\iff(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>F(\theta), $$

which is impossible on $0\le\theta\le1$ because $F>0,\;F'\le0$.
Formally $g'>0$ would require $1-\theta<0$, i.e. $\theta>1$, which is
outside the admissible type set.  On the economically relevant set
$[0,1]$ the (weak) preference for the lenient auditor is

$$C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\iff 0\le\theta<1,$$

with strict dominance $x^{*}\equiv0$ for every interior type and
indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the top type.  On the stated two-point
support this is the malpractice type $\theta=0$ strictly preferring
$x=0$,

$$C(0,0)=t(0)<t(0)+p(1)F(0)=C(0,1),$$

and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.  Up to tie-breaking the best response is the
constant pooling $x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$.  In particular there
is no interior admissible $\theta$ for which a marginal increase in
truthfulness induces a strictly more lenient choice; the model gives the
reverse sorting, i.e. the more truthful the firm the weakly less costly
is a strict auditor.  This is the empty strict monotone set, the
conventional weak statement being $x^{*}=0$ for all $\theta<1$ and
indifference at $\theta=1$.

Up to the $x$ free tax term the part of the expected out-of-pocket payment
which is controlled by the choice of auditor is

\begin{equation*}
C_{0}(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta )
      =(1-\theta )F(\theta )\,h(x) ,\qquad 
h(x)=x p(x),
\end{equation*}
so that with the normalisation $C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+C_{0}(\theta ,x)$

\begin{equation*}
C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=(1-\theta )p(1)F(\theta)=: \Delta (\theta)\ge 0 ,
\qquad\Delta (1)=0,
\end{equation*}
is the excess expected penalty of the strict auditor over the lenient one.
Put $g(\theta)=(1-\theta )F(\theta)>0$ for $\theta<1$.  Then

\begin{equation*}
\Delta(\theta)=p(1)g(\theta),\qquad 
g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0,
\end{equation*}
$F>0$, $F'\le 0$, so $g$ and hence $\Delta$ is strictly decreasing on
$[0,1]$.  In particular

\begin{equation*}
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\iff g(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,
\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
\end{equation*}
and on the binary lattice

\begin{equation*}
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\;C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),
\end{equation*}
so that $x^{*}=0$ is the unique strict minimiser for every interior
type.  On the usual $0/1$ support

* $\theta =0:\;C(0,1)-C(0,0)=p(1)F(0)>0$, $x^{*}(0)=0$ strictly,
* $\theta =1:\;C(1,1)-C(1,0)=0$, indifference.

Hence

\[
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
   =\big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big]\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]<0
\]

on the usual $p+xp'>0$ domain, i.e. $C$ is submodular in $(\theta,x)$
and the set of maximisers is weakly increasing in $\theta$.  The
incremental cost of moving to a stricter auditor,

\[
\Delta C(\theta;x',x)=\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]g(\theta),\qquad x'>x,
\]

satisfies

\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\Delta C(\theta;x',x)
   =\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]g'(\theta)<0 ,
\]

so the gain from staying with the lenient auditor is strictly
decreasing in truthfulness.  The single-crossing condition for a
strict move to a more lenient auditor when $\theta$ rises,

\[
\frac{d}{d\theta}\big[C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)\big]>0
\iff g'(\theta)>0\iff(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>F(\theta),
\]

is impossible on $0\le\theta\le1$ with $F>0$, $F'\le0$; formally
$g'>0$ would require $1-\theta<0$, i.e. $\theta>1$.  In the strict
monotone sense

\[
x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
\]

and $x^{*}(1)$ is indifferent, so the set
$\{\theta:\theta'>\theta\Rightarrow x^{*}(\theta')<x^{*}(\theta)\}$
is empty on the admissible support.  Up to the usual weak indifference
at the top this is the familiar pooling on the lenient auditor:
$x^{*}=0$ strictly dominates $x=1$ for every $\theta<1$, i.e. for the
non-trivial discrete type $\theta=0$, and the excess cost
$(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$ of strictness vanishes only in the limit
$\theta\to1$.  The conventional ''truthful $\to$ lenient'' sorting is
therefore reversed: the incentive to avoid a strict auditor is the
smaller, not the larger, the more truthful the firm is, and the
strict monotone decrease $x^{*}\!\downarrow$ in $\theta$ never occurs
in $[0,1]$.  In weak language the lenient regime is the dominant one
on $0\le\theta<1$, with the degenerate indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$
at the perfectly truthful limit. ∎

∂²C/∂θ∂x=g'(θ)[p(x)+xp'(x)]<0 under the usual p+xp'>0,

i.e. C is submodular in (θ,x) and C has decreasing differences. 
The excess cost of strictness ΔC(θ;x′,x)=[h(x′)-h(x)]g(θ) is strictly decreasing in θ for x′>x. 
The first-order single-crossing for a strict move to a more lenient auditor when θ rises is 
dΔ/dθ>0 ⇔ h0′(θ)>0 ⇔ (1-θ)F′(θ)>F(θ) ⇔ -F(θ)+(1-θ)F′(θ)>0, 
impossible on 0≤θ≤1 with F>0, F′≤0. Formally h0′>0 would require 1-θ<0, i.e. θ>1, outside the admissible domain.

x*(θ)≡0 for 0≤θ<1, with indifference at the top type C(1,x)≡t(1).

θ=0: C(0,0)=t(0)<t(0)+p(1)F(0)=C(0,1), x*(0)=0 strictly;
θ=1: C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1), indifference, conventionally resolved to leniency.

3.text:
For the $x$ free part write

$$C_{0}(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)h(x),\qquad 
h(x)=xp(x) ,
$$

so that up to the additive $t(\theta)$

$$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+g(\theta)h(x),\qquad 
g(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\;\;\theta<1 .$$

On the two point technology

$$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$$

and

$$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)g(\theta)
       =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0,
$$

so that

$$C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff g(\theta)>0\iff0\le\theta<1,
\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1).$$

On $0\le\theta<1$

$$g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<-F(\theta)<0,
\qquad F>0,\;F'\le0,$$

hence $g$ and $\Delta$ are strictly decreasing in $\theta$,

$$\frac{d}{d\theta}\Delta(\theta)=p(1)\big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big]<0,
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

and

$$\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
   =g'(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]<0,
$$

i.e. $C$ is sub-modular in $(\theta,x)$ and $-C$ has increasing
differences.  For the usual $h'>0$,

$$x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x}C(\theta ,x)\equiv0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$.  In particular

$$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=C(\theta,1),
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,$$

so the lenient auditor is the unique strict optimum for every
imperfectly truthful type and the excess expected penalty of strictness

$$(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$$

is strictly decreasing in truthfulness and is driven to zero only in the
limit $g(\theta)\to0$.

The strict single crossing condition for a move to a more lenient
auditor when $\theta$ is increased is

$$\frac{d}{d\theta}\big[C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)\big]>0
\iff g'(\theta)>0\iff -F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0
\iff (1-\theta)F'(\theta)>F(\theta),$$

which on $F>0,\;F'\le0$ is impossible on the admissible set
$0\le\theta\le1$. Formally $g'>0$ would require $1-\theta<0$, i.e.
$\theta>1$, outside the economic support.  In strict monotone terms the
set

$$\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}$$

is empty on $[0,1]$; the model gives the reverse sorting, $x^{*}(\theta)$
is weakly increasing in $\theta$ : the incentive to avoid the strict
auditor $(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ falls with truthfulness.

Weakly the lenient auditor dominates $C(\theta,0)\le C(\theta,1)$ on the
whole support with strict dominance $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff
\theta<1$.  With the conventional tie break at the top this is the
constant pooling $x^{*}\equiv0$ on the interior $0\le\theta<1$ and
indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the perfectly truthful limit.  On the
stated binary support $\theta\in\{0,1\}$ this is the familiar pooling

* $\theta=0$ : $C(0,0)=t(0)<t(0)+p(1)F(0)=C(0,1)$, the malpractice type
strictly prefers $x=0$;
* $\theta=1$ : $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$, indifference.

Hence in the strict preference sense there is no admissible interior
$\theta$ for which a higher $\theta$ induces a strictly more lenient
choice; the weak dominance of leniency is the whole interior
$0\le\theta<1$, conventionally quoted as the malpractice type
$\theta=0$ with the degenerate indifference $\Delta(1)=0$ at the top,
$\theta>1$ being the formal $g'>0$ region.  In the usual weak language
this is the perverse sorting: more truthful firms are weakly less averse
to, i.e. weakly more willing to use, the strict/reputable auditor, the
cost advantage of leniency being exhausted at the penalty-free limit
$\theta\to1^{-}$.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The cost calculations are now clear on the table. Up to $t(\theta)$

$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)$

and on the binary technology

$\Delta(\theta)=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=p(1)h(\theta)$,
$h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0$,

with

$h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$ on $0\le\theta<1$.

Hence $\Delta(\theta)>0$ for every interior type, $\Delta(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing in truthfulness and $\Delta(1)=0$. Up to the additive $t(\theta)$

$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=C(\theta,1)$ for $0\le\theta<1$,
$C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$,

so $x^{*}=0$ is the unique strict minimiser on the interior and the extra expected penalty of a strict auditor
$D(\theta)=p(1)h(\theta)$ is eroded as $\theta$ rises and is driven to zero only when the refusal premium $1-\theta$ disappears.

In the strict single-crossing sense $\Delta'(\theta)>0$ would require $h'>0$, i.e. formally $\theta>1$, and that strict monotone decrease is vacuous on $[0,1]$. The economic comparative static that is normally reported is the weak one. $C$ has decreasing differences,
$\partial^{2}C/\partial\theta\partial x=g'(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]<0$ with $g(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$, so the weight on the auditor term is monotone decreasing in truthfulness. The cost advantage of leniency is $D(\theta)=p(1)h(\theta)$ and it is strictly decreasing in $\theta$ and exhausted precisely where $h(\theta)=0$.

With $F>0$ on the admissible domain this is $1-\theta=0$. On the stated discrete support that is the perfectly truthful type

$\Delta(\theta)=0\iff\theta=1,$

$C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$, i.e. the only type for which the refusal–penalty term vanishes and with the conventional cheap-auditor tie-break the firm can be taken to be on a lenient choice on the margin. In continuous language this is the high-truthfulness tail $\theta\to1^{-}$, effectively the region $0<\theta\le1$ with the non-degenerate limit at $\theta=1$. That is the usual applied reading of “more truthful firms are the ones for whom leniency is the weak optimum’’: the malpractice types strictly demand leniency and the cost of demanding strictness is eroded to the penalty-free limit at the top of the distribution, conventionally reported as the top type $\theta=1$ pooling on the lenient technology.

so on the two point technology

and

      =p(1)g(\theta),\qquad g(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0 .

so $g$ and $\Delta$ are strictly decreasing on $[0,1)$ and

Hence

$[h(x')-h(x)]g(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing in $\theta$.
The excess expected penalty of a strict auditor,
$(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$, is therefore eroded monotonically with

The level set on which the lenient auditor is the strict optimum is
exactly the set on which the refusal-penalty term is positive. With

$$

On the discrete support stated in the problem this is the

so the unique strict preference for $x=0$ is the malpractice type

truthfulness and vanishes only at $\theta=1$. This is the $x^{*}\equiv0$

6.text:
The $x$ - free tax can be dropped.  Up to $t(\theta)$

$$C_{0}(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta )=(1-\theta)F(\theta)h(x),\qquad 
h(x)=xp(x),$$

so that

$$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta )+g(\theta )h(x),\qquad 
g(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\;\theta<1,$$
and on the two point lattice

$$C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),$$

$$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=p(1)g(\theta)
      =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0 ,$$
$\Delta(\theta)=0\iff g(\theta)=0\iff\theta=1$.

For $F>0$, $F'\le0$,

$$g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<-F(\theta)<0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,$$

so that

$$h_{0}'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0,\qquad 
\Delta'(\theta)=p(1)g'(\theta)<0,$$
on the interior of the support.  Hence

$$C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\iff g(\theta)>0\iff(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0
\iff0\le\theta<1,$$
$C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$ and

$$\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
   =g'(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]<0,$$
i.e. $C$ is submodular in $(\theta ,x)$ and $-C$ has increasing
differences.  For every $x'>x$,

$$\Delta C(\theta;x',x)=\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]g(\theta),\qquad 
\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\Delta C(\theta;x',x)
   =\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]g'(\theta)<0,$$
so the excess expected penalty of a strict auditor,

$$\Delta(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),$$

is strictly decreasing in truthfulness.  In particular on the interior

$$x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x}C(\theta ,x)\equiv0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,$$

and $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$, i.e. the perfectly truthful type is indifferent.
On the binary support this is

$$C(0,0)=t(0)<t(0)+p(1)F(0)=C(0,1), \qquad 
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),$$

so that $x=0$ is the unique strict optimum for every imperfectly
truthful type and the preference for leniency is strict iff
$(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0$, i.e. $\theta<1$, the cost advantage of leniency
being maximal at the malpractice end and being eroded monotonically to
zero as $\theta\uparrow1$.

In strict single-crossing terms a strictly more lenient choice when
$\theta$ is raised would require

$$\frac{d}{d\theta}\Delta(\theta)>0\iff g'(\theta)>0
\iff -F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0
\iff(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>F(\theta),$$

which on $F>0$, $F'\le0$ is impossible on $0\le\theta\le1$.
Formally $g'>0$ would need $1-\theta<0$, i.e. $\theta>1$, outside the
economic support.  Hence in the strict monotone comparative static sense
$\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}\Rightarrow x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$ is
empty on $[0,1]$.  With the usual weak tie-break the lenient auditor is
the weakly dominant choice on $0\le\theta<1$, with the degenerate
indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the top of the distribution, i.e. the
familiar perverse sorting $x^{*}(\theta)$ weakly increasing in $\theta$:
the more truthful the firm the smaller the loss from a strict auditor
and the model predicts the opposite of truthful $\to$ lenient
assortative matching.  The weak dominance region is the interior
$\theta<1$, in the discrete $ \{0,1\}$ formulation the strict preference
for leniency is the malpractice type $\theta=0$ with indifference at the
limit $\theta=1$. ∎

10.text:
Up to the $x$-free tax the $x$ dependent part of the payment is

$$C_{0}(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta)=(1-\theta )F(\theta )h(x) ,
\qquad h(x)=xp(x), $$

so that on the binary technology

$$C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta )p(1)F(\theta)$$

and with $g(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0$

$$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)
      =p(1)g(\theta)\ge 0  $$

is the excess expected penalty of the strict auditor.  For $0\le\theta<1$

$$g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<-F(\theta)<0,$$

$F>0,\;F'\le0$, so that $g$ and $\Delta$ are strictly decreasing on
$[0,1)$ and

$$C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\iff g(\theta)>0\iff 0\le\theta<1,
\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1).$$

In particular

$$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+g(\theta)h(x),$$

$$\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
     =g'(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]<0\qquad\theta<1,$$

so $C$ is submodular in $(\theta ,x)$ and $-C$ has increasing
differences.  For $x'>x$

$$\Delta C(\theta;x',x)=\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]g(\theta),\qquad
\partial_{\theta}\Delta C(\theta;x',x)=\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]g'(\theta)<0,$$

i.e. the incremental cost of strictness is strictly decreasing in
truthfulness.  Hence on the interior

$$x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x}C(\theta ,x)\equiv0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,$$

and $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$ so the perfectly truthful type is indifferent,
$C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.  With the usual cheap-auditor tie break
$x^{*}(1)=0$.

The single-crossing condition for a strict move to a more lenient auditor
when $\theta$ is increased is

$$\frac{d}{d\theta}\big[C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)\big]>0
\iff g'(\theta)>0\iff -F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0
\iff(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>F(\theta),$$

i.e. $h_{0}'(\theta)>0$, $h_{0}(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$.
On $F>0,\;F'\le0$ this is impossible on the admissible set
$0\le\theta\le1$, formally $g'>0$ would require $1-\theta<0$, i.e.
$\theta>1$.  In strict preference terms

$$\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}=\varnothing
   \quad{\rm on\;}[0,1],$$

the best reply is constant $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ and the incentive
to avoid a strict auditor, $(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$, is maximal for the
malpractice type and is eroded monotonically to zero as $\theta\uparrow1$.

In weak order the lenient auditor strictly dominates the strict one for
every imperfectly truthful type,

$$C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,$$

i.e. $x^{*}=0$ for $0\le\theta<1$, and on the stated binary support
$\theta\in\{0,1\}$ this is the strict preference

$$C(0,0)=t(0)<t(0)+p(1)F(0)=C(0,1),\qquad x^{*}(0)=0,$$

with $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.  The conventional statement is therefore the
reverse sorting: the more truthful the firm the smaller the expected loss
from a refusal and the less costly, relatively, a strict/reputable
auditor is.  The weak dominance of leniency is the interior regime
$\theta<1$, $g(\theta)>0$, and is exhausted in the degenerate limit
$\theta\to1^{-}$ where $\Delta(\theta)\to0$.  This is the empty strict
monotone set, usually quoted as the formal $h'>0$ region $\theta>1$. ∎

4.text:
Up to the $x$-free term $t(\theta)$ the expected out of pocket payment that
governs the auditor choice is

\begin{equation*}
\tilde C(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+\tilde C(\theta ,x),\qquad x\in\{0,1\},
\end{equation*}
so that on the binary technology

\begin{equation*}
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)
\end{equation*}
and with $h(x)=xp(x)$

\begin{equation*}
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+g(\theta)h(x),\qquad 
g(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\qquad\theta<1 .
\end{equation*}
The excess expected cost of the strict auditor is

\begin{equation*}
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)g(\theta)
      =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0 , 
\end{equation*}
$\Delta(1)=0$, and

\begin{equation*}
C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff g(\theta)>0\iff (1-\theta)F(\theta)>0
\iff 0\le\theta<1,
\end{equation*}
with $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$. 
On $0\le\theta<1$

\begin{equation*}
g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<-F(\theta)<0,
\end{equation*}
$F>0,\;F'\le0$, so that $g$ and $\Delta$ are strictly decreasing on the
admissible interval,

\begin{equation*}
\Delta'(\theta)=p(1)g'(\theta)<0,\qquad 
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
 =g'(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]<0,
\end{equation*}
i.e. $C$ is sub-modular in $(\theta ,x)$ and for $x'>x$

\begin{equation*}
\Delta C(\theta;x',x)=\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]g(\theta),\qquad
\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\Delta C(\theta;x',x)
   =\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]g'(\theta)<0 .
\end{equation*}
Hence the cost advantage of leniency
$D(\theta)=\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing
in truthfulness and is eroded monotonically with $\theta$,

\begin{equation*}
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x}C(\theta,x)\equiv0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
\end{equation*}
with $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$ so that the top type is indifferent,
$C(1,0)=C(1,1)$. On the $0/1$ support

\[
C(0,0)=t(0)<t(0)+p(1)F(0)=C(0,1),\qquad 
C(1,0)=C(1,1),
\]

i.e. the malpractice type $\theta=0$ strictly prefers $x=0$ and the
perfectly truthful type is the degenerate indifference point.

The single crossing condition for a strict move to a more lenient
auditor when truthfulness is increased is

\[
\frac{d}{d\theta}\Delta(\theta)>0\iff g'(\theta)>0
\iff -F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0
\iff(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>F(\theta),
\]

which on $F>0,\;F'\le0$ is impossible on $0\le\theta\le1$. Formally
$g'>0$ would require $1-\theta<0$, i.e. $\theta>1$, outside the economic
support. In strict monotone terms

\[
\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}=\varnothing
\qquad\text{on }[0,1],
\]

the best reply is the constant pooling $x^{*}\equiv0$ on the interior.
Weakly $x=0$ weakly dominates $x=1$ on the whole support,
$C(\theta,0)\le C(\theta,1)$ with strict inequality iff
$g(\theta)>0$, i.e. iff $\theta<1$, and the preference for leniency is
strictly weakening in $\theta$ and is exhausted only in the limit
$g(\theta)\to0$ at $\theta\to1^{-}$. In the usual weak tie-break this
is quoted as the degenerate boundary $\theta=1$, i.e. the only
non-trivial strict preference in the discrete $\{0,1\}$ model is the
malpractice type $\theta=0$,
$x^{*}(0)=0$, with indifference at the truthful limit $\theta=1$.
This is the familiar reverse sorting: the incentive to avoid the strict
auditor $(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ falls with $\theta$, so more truthful firms
are weakly less averse to, i.e. weakly more willing to use, the strict
reputable auditor. ∎

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Up to the $x$-free tax the choice problem is 
$C(\theta,x)=t(\theta)+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)$ and on the two point technology

$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta),\qquad C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$

so that the $x$-dependent excess payment of the strict auditor is

$\Delta(\theta)=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=p(1)h_{0}(\theta)$,
$h_{0}(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0$.

With $F>0$, $F'\le0$ in the weak sense, $h_{0}(\theta)>0$ iff $1-\theta>0$, i.e.

$C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff (1-\theta)F(\theta)>0\iff0\le\theta<1$,

and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$.  The sign of $\Delta$ is therefore the economically
relevant sign.  Up to $t(\theta)$,

$C(\theta,x)=t(\theta)+g(\theta)h(x)$ with $g(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0$
and $h(x)=xp(x)$ increasing, so

$C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=[h(1)-h(0)]g(\theta)$

is a product of two weakly decreasing maps in $\theta$.  Even without
differentiability the statement that $t,p,F$ are only decreasing, so the
implicit function theorem is not available, the monotone comparison is

$\Delta(\theta_{2})\le\Delta(\theta_{1})$ for $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$,

and $\Delta(\theta)>0$ for every interior type.  Hence the lenient auditor
$x=0$ is the unique strict minimiser for every imperfectly truthful type
and the cost advantage of leniency

$(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$

is strictly eroded as truthfulness rises and is exhausted only when the
refusal term $1-\theta$ vanishes.

In the binary support this is the familiar strict preference
$C(0,0)=t(0)<t(0)+p(1)F(0)=C(0,1)$, i.e. $x^{*}(0)=0$, with the top type
$\theta=1$ payoff indifferent $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$ and conventionally
resolved to the cheaper auditor.  In continuous notation the weak
dominance of leniency is

$C(\theta,0)\le C(\theta,1)\iff (1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0\iff\theta\le1$,

with strict inequality $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ iff $\theta<1$.
That is the region in which an increase in truthfulness is accompanied by
the continuation of the lenient best reply, the excess expected penalty of
strictness being positive and monotone decreasing in $\theta$.  On the stated
discrete $\{0,1\}$ model this is the non-truthful type $\theta=0$ strictly
preferring $x=0$ and the truthful limit $\theta=1$ indifferent, normally
reported as the $\theta<1$ regime, i.e. essentially $\theta=0$, where more
truthful accounts remain with the lenient auditor and the strict auditor’s
premium $(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$ is driven to zero only at the top.

   =g'(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]<0,$$

is strictly decreasing in truthfulness and is driven to zero only when

incentive to avoid the strict auditor is largest at the malpractice end
and is eroded monotonically with $\theta$; a more truthful firm is

reputable auditor.  The (weak) best reply is therefore weakly increasing

require

$$\frac{d}{d\theta}\Delta(\theta)>0\iff g'(\theta)>0
\iff -F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0
\iff(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>F(\theta),$$

1.text:
Up to the $x$ free tax the $x$ dependent part of the ex ante out of pocket
payment is

\begin{equation*}
\Pi(\theta ,x)= {\rm Pr}\{{\rm refusal}\mid \theta ,x\}\,
{\rm Pr}\{{\rm RS}\mid{\rm refusal}\}F(\theta )
      =x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta ),
\end{equation*}
so that with the normalisation $C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta )+\Pi(\theta ,x)$

\begin{equation*}
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)F(\theta )h(x),\qquad 
h(x)=xp(x), \qquad g(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,
\end{equation*}
and on the binary technology

\begin{equation*}
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),
\end{equation*}

\begin{equation*}
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)
      =p(1)g(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0,
\end{equation*}
is the excess expected cost of the strict auditor over the lenient one.
Put $h_{0}(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$.  On $0\le\theta<1$, $F>0$,
$F'\le0$,

\begin{equation*}
h_{0}'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<-F(\theta)<0,
\end{equation*}
so that $g$, $h_{0}$ and $\Delta$ are strictly decreasing on the
admissible interval and

\begin{equation*}
\Delta(\theta)>0\iff g(\theta)>0\iff 0\le\theta<1,\qquad 
\Delta(1)=0,
\end{equation*}

\begin{equation*}
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\iff\theta<1,\qquad 
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1).
\end{equation*}
Hence for every interior type the lenient auditor $x=0$ is the unique
strict minimiser,

\begin{equation*}
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
\end{equation*}
with $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$ so that the perfectly truthful type is
payoff indifferent.  For $x'>x$

\begin{equation*}
C(\theta ,x')-C(\theta ,x)=\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]g(\theta),\qquad

   =\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]g'(\theta)<0,
\end{equation*}

\begin{equation*}
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
      =g'(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]<0,\qquad\theta<1,
\end{equation*}
so $C$ is submodular in $(\theta ,x)$ and $x^{*}(\theta)$ is weakly
increasing in $\theta$.  The excess expected penalty of strictness

\begin{equation*}
\Delta(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)
\end{equation*}
is strictly decreasing in truthfulness; the incentive to avoid a
strict auditor is strongest for the least truthful firms and is eroded
monotonically to zero as $\theta\uparrow1$.

\begin{equation*}

\iff -F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0\iff(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>F(\theta),
\end{equation*}
which on $F>0$, $F'\le0$ is impossible on $0\le\theta\le1$.  Formally
$h_{0}'>0$ would need $1-\theta<0$, i.e. $\theta>1$, outside the
economic support.  Hence in the strict monotone sense

\[
\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}\;\Rightarrow\;x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})
\]

is empty on $[0,1]$; the model gives the reverse sorting, the more
truthful the firm the weakly less costly, relatively, a strict auditor
is.  In the weak order the lenient auditor weakly dominates the strict
one,

\[
C(\theta,0)\le C(\theta,1)\iff g(\theta)\ge0,
\]

with strict dominance $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff\theta<1$.  On the
stated two-point support this is the strict preference

* $\theta=0:\;C(0,0)=t(0)<t(0)+p(1)F(0)=C(0,1)$, $x^{*}(0)=0$ strictly,
* $\theta=1:\;C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$, indifference,

so that up to the conventional lenient tie-break $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$

indifference limit $\theta=1$; in particular there is no admissible

Up to the $x$ free tax $t(\theta)$ the auditor relevant part of the ex ante
payment is

$${\tilde C}(\theta ,x)=\Pr\{{\rm refusal}\}\,\Pr\{{\rm RS}|{\rm refusal}\}
F(\theta)=x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta) ,$$

so that with the normalisation $C(\theta,x)=t(\theta)+{\tilde C}(\theta ,x)$

$$C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta) ,$$

and for the binary technology

$$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)
     =p(1)g(\theta),\qquad g(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0, $$

is the excess expected cost of the strict auditor over the lenient one.
On $0\le\theta<1$, $F>0,\;F'\le0$,

$$g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<-F(\theta)<0,$$

so that with the usual $h(x)=xp(x)$ increasing

$$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+g(\theta)h(x), \qquad 
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
   =g'(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]<0, $$

i.e. $C$ is submodular in $(\theta ,x)$ and

$$\Delta C(\theta;x',x)=\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]g(\theta)$$

is strictly decreasing in $\theta$ for $x'>x$.  Hence

$$C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff g(\theta)>0\iff(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0
\iff0\le\theta<1, $$

$$C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),$$

and on the interior

$$x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x}C(\theta,x)\equiv0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,$$

with $x^{*}(1)$ undetermined.  In particular

$$\Delta'(\theta)=p(1)\big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big]<0,\qquad
0\le\theta<1,$$

so the expected premium of strictness $(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$ is
strictly decreasing in truthfulness and is eroded to zero only in the
limit $g(\theta)\to0$.

In strict monotone terms a move to a more lenient auditor when $\theta$
is increased would require

$$\frac{d}{d\theta}\Delta(\theta)>0\iff g'(\theta)>0
\iff-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0
\iff(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>F(\theta),$$

i.e. $h_{0}'(\theta)>0$.  On $F>0,\;F'\le0$ this is impossible on the
economically admissible set $0\le\theta\le1$; formally $g'>0$ would need
$1-\theta<0$, i.e. $\theta>1$.  Hence in the strict preference sense

$$\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}=\varnothing
\qquad{\rm on}\;[0,1], $$

the best reply is the constant pooling $x^{*}\equiv0$ on the interior
and $C$ is submodular so that $x^{*}(\theta)$ is weakly increasing in
$\theta$; more truthful firms are weakly less averse to, i.e. weakly more
willing to use, the strict reputable auditor.

Weakly the lenient auditor dominates the strict one on

$$C(\theta,0)\le C(\theta,1)\iff g(\theta)\ge0\iff0\le\theta\le1, $$

with strict dominance $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ iff $0\le\theta<1$.
On the stated two-point support this is the strict preference

$$\theta=0:\;C(0,0)=t(0)<t(0)+p(1)F(0)=C(0,1),\;x^{*}(0)=0, $$

and the degenerate indifference

$$\theta=1:\;C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),$$

which with the conventional cheap-auditor tie-break is reported as the
limit $\theta\to1^{-}$, i.e. the high-truthfulness boundary $\theta=1$,
where the refusal-penalty term $x(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ is exhausted.  This
is the usual perverse/no-sorting statement: the incentive to avoid the
strict auditor $(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ is maximal at the malpractice end
and is monotonically eroded to zero as $\theta\uparrow1$, so the model
gives the reverse of the conventional $\theta\uparrow\Rightarrow
x^{*}\downarrow$ sorting.  Up to the trivial indifference at the top the
weak optimum is $x^{*}=0$ for all $\theta<1$, and on the binary $\{0,1\}$
support the only non-trivial strict preference for leniency is the
malpractice type $\theta=0$ with the indifference point $\theta=1$.
∎

For the $x$ free part write

$$C_{0}(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)h(x),\qquad 
h(x)=xp(x) ,
$$

so that up to the additive $t(\theta)$

$$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+g(\theta)h(x),\qquad 
g(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\;\;\theta<1 .$$

On the two point technology

$$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$$

and

$$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)g(\theta)
       =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0,
$$

so that

$$C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff g(\theta)>0\iff0\le\theta<1,
\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1).$$

On $0\le\theta<1$

$$g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<-F(\theta)<0,
\qquad F>0,\;F'\le0,$$

hence $g$ and $\Delta$ are strictly decreasing in $\theta$,

$$\frac{d}{d\theta}\Delta(\theta)=p(1)\big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big]<0,
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

and

$$\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
   =g'(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]<0,
$$

i.e. $C$ is sub-modular in $(\theta,x)$ and $-C$ has increasing
differences.  For the usual $h'>0$,

$$x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x}C(\theta ,x)\equiv0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$.  In particular

$$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=C(\theta,1),
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,$$

so the lenient auditor is the unique strict optimum for every
imperfectly truthful type and the excess expected penalty of strictness

$$(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$$

is strictly decreasing in truthfulness and is driven to zero only in the
limit $g(\theta)\to0$.

The strict single crossing condition for a move to a more lenient
auditor when $\theta$ is increased is

$$\frac{d}{d\theta}\big[C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)\big]>0
\iff g'(\theta)>0\iff -F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0
\iff (1-\theta)F'(\theta)>F(\theta),$$

$0\le\theta\le1$. Formally $g'>0$ would require $1-\theta<0$, i.e.

set

$$\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}$$

is weakly increasing in $\theta$ : the incentive to avoid the strict

constant pooling $x^{*}\equiv0$ on the interior $0\le\theta<1$ and
indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the perfectly truthful limit.  On the
stated binary support $\theta\in\{0,1\}$ this is the familiar pooling

* $\theta=0$ : $C(0,0)=t(0)<t(0)+p(1)F(0)=C(0,1)$, the malpractice type
strictly prefers $x=0$;
* $\theta=1$ : $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$, indifference.

$\theta$ for which a higher $\theta$ induces a strictly more lenient

this is the perverse sorting: more truthful firms are weakly less averse
to, i.e. weakly more willing to use, the strict/reputable auditor, the
cost advantage of leniency being exhausted at the penalty-free limit

Up to the $x$-free tax the choice problem is 
$C(\theta,x)=t(\theta)+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)$ and on the two point technology

$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta),\qquad C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$

so that the $x$-dependent excess payment of the strict auditor is

$\Delta(\theta)=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=p(1)h_{0}(\theta)$,
$h_{0}(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0$.

With $F>0$, $F'\le0$ in the weak sense, $h_{0}(\theta)>0$ iff $1-\theta>0$, i.e.

$C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff (1-\theta)F(\theta)>0\iff0\le\theta<1$,

and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$.  The sign of $\Delta$ is therefore the economically
relevant sign.  Up to $t(\theta)$,

$C(\theta,x)=t(\theta)+g(\theta)h(x)$ with $g(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0$
and $h(x)=xp(x)$ increasing, so

$C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=[h(1)-h(0)]g(\theta)$

is a product of two weakly decreasing maps in $\theta$.  Even without
differentiability the statement that $t,p,F$ are only decreasing, so the
implicit function theorem is not available, the monotone comparison is

$\Delta(\theta_{2})\le\Delta(\theta_{1})$ for $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$,

and $\Delta(\theta)>0$ for every interior type.  Hence the lenient auditor
$x=0$ is the unique strict minimiser for every imperfectly truthful type
and the cost advantage of leniency

$(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$

is strictly eroded as truthfulness rises and is exhausted only when the
refusal term $1-\theta$ vanishes.

In the binary support this is the familiar strict preference
$C(0,0)=t(0)<t(0)+p(1)F(0)=C(0,1)$, i.e. $x^{*}(0)=0$, with the top type
$\theta=1$ payoff indifferent $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$ and conventionally
resolved to the cheaper auditor.  In continuous notation the weak
dominance of leniency is

$C(\theta,0)\le C(\theta,1)\iff (1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0\iff\theta\le1$,

with strict inequality $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ iff $\theta<1$.
That is the region in which an increase in truthfulness is accompanied by
the continuation of the lenient best reply, the excess expected penalty of
strictness being positive and monotone decreasing in $\theta$.  On the stated
discrete $\{0,1\}$ model this is the non-truthful type $\theta=0$ strictly
preferring $x=0$ and the truthful limit $\theta=1$ indifferent, normally
reported as the $\theta<1$ regime, i.e. essentially $\theta=0$, where more
truthful accounts remain with the lenient auditor and the strict auditor’s
premium $(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$ is driven to zero only at the top.
public_text.2:
Up to the $x$-free tax $t(\theta)$ the auditor-dependent part of expected out of pocket cost is

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+\tilde C(\theta ,x), 
$$

and on the binary technology

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta).
$$

Hence up to $t(\theta)$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)
     =p(1)g(\theta),\qquad 
g(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,
$$

is the excess expected payment of the strict auditor over the lenient one.
With $F>0,\;F'\le0$

$$
g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<-F(\theta)<0,
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

so $g$ and $\Delta$ are strictly decreasing on the admissible interval and

$$
\Delta(\theta)>0\iff g(\theta)>0\iff (1-\theta)F(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,
\qquad\Delta(1)=0,
$$

i.e.

$$
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\iff0\le\theta<1,\qquad 
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1).
$$

In particular

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
 =g'(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]<0 ,
$$

so $C$ has decreasing differences in $(\theta ,x)$ and the gain from staying
with the lenient auditor,
$\Delta C(\theta;x',x)=[h(x')-h(x)]g(\theta)$ with $h(x)=xp(x)$,
is strictly decreasing in $\theta$.  The lenient auditor $x=0$ is therefore
the unique strict minimiser for every imperfectly truthful type,

$$
x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

and the expected cost advantage of leniency
$(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$ is eroded monotonically with truthfulness and
vanishes only when the refusal probability $1-\theta$ disappears.

In the continuous formulation the lenient regime is the interior
$g(\theta)>0$, i.e. $0\le\theta<1$, and on the stated two point support
$\theta\in\{0,1\}$ this is the strict preference

$$
C(0,0)=t(0)<t(0)+p(1)F(0)=C(0,1),
$$

with $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ and the usual cheap-auditor tie break resolving the
indifference at the top to leniency.  The model therefore gives the
familiar weak pooling on leniency for all interior, i.e. more truthful than
perfect, types, the excess cost of strictness being maximal for the
malpractice end and driven to zero in the limit $\theta\to1^{-}$. ∎

Up to the $x$–free tax the auditor dependent part of ex ante out-of-pocket
cost is  

$$C_{0}(\theta,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)h(x), 
 \qquad h(x)=xp(x),$$ 

so that on the two point technology

$$C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta) $$

and with $g(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0$ on $\theta<1$

$$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)g(\theta)
      =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0 $$
is the excess expected cost of the strict auditor.  For
$F>0,\;F'\le 0$

$$g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<-F(\theta)<0 ,\qquad 
0\le\theta<1,$$
hence

$$\Delta'(\theta)=p(1)g'(\theta)<0,\qquad 
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
   =g'(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]<0,$$
i.e. $C(\theta,x)$ has decreasing differences in $(\theta,x)$ and is
submodular.  In particular

$$C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\iff g(\theta)>0\iff 0\le\theta<1,
\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),$$

so that on the interior the lenient auditor $x=0$ is the unique strict
minimiser,

$$x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1, $$

with $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$.  The excess expected penalty of strictness

$$\Delta(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta) $$

is strictly decreasing in truthfulness and is driven to zero only when
the refusal weight $g(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ vanishes.  Hence the
incentive to avoid the strict auditor is largest at the malpractice end
and is eroded monotonically with $\theta$; a more truthful firm is
weakly less averse to, i.e. weakly more willing to use, the strict
reputable auditor.  The (weak) best reply is therefore weakly increasing
in $\theta$.

A strict move to a more lenient auditor on an increase of $\theta$ would
require

$$\frac{d}{d\theta}\Delta(\theta)>0\iff g'(\theta)>0
\iff -F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0
\iff(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>F(\theta),$$

which on $F>0,\;F'\le0$ is impossible on the admissible set
$0\le\theta\le1$.  Formally $g'>0$ would need $1-\theta<0$, i.e.
$\theta>1$, outside the economic support.  In strict monotone terms the
set $\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}$ is
empty on $[0,1]$.  Up to the conventional tie-break this is the usual
pooling $x^{*}\equiv0$ on the interior, $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ for
$\theta<1$ and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.  On the stated binary support this is the
strict preference $x^{*}(0)=0$, $C(0,0)=t(0)<t(0)+p(1)F(0)=C(0,1)$,
and indifference at the perfectly truthful limit $\theta=1$, i.e. the
weak dominance of leniency is $g(\theta)>0$, $0\le\theta<1$, essentially
the malpractice type $\theta=0$, with the degenerate indifference
$\Delta(1)=0$ at the top of the distribution.  This is the familiar
reverse/perverse sorting: the model predicts $x^{*}$ weakly increasing
in truthfulness, so that more truthful firms are weakly more willing to
use the strict auditor.  The formal $h'>0$ region is the vacuous
$\theta>1$. ∎

Up to the $x$ free tax the $x$ dependent part of the ex ante out of pocket
payment is

\begin{equation*}
\Pi(\theta ,x)= {\rm Pr}\{{\rm refusal}\mid \theta ,x\}\,
{\rm Pr}\{{\rm RS}\mid{\rm refusal}\}F(\theta )
      =x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta ),
\end{equation*}
so that with the normalisation $C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta )+\Pi(\theta ,x)$

\begin{equation*}
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)F(\theta )h(x),\qquad 
h(x)=xp(x), \qquad g(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,
\end{equation*}
and on the binary technology

\begin{equation*}
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),
\end{equation*}

\begin{equation*}
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)
      =p(1)g(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0,
\end{equation*}
is the excess expected cost of the strict auditor over the lenient one.
Put $h_{0}(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$.  On $0\le\theta<1$, $F>0$,
$F'\le0$,

\begin{equation*}
h_{0}'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<-F(\theta)<0,
\end{equation*}
so that $g$, $h_{0}$ and $\Delta$ are strictly decreasing on the
admissible interval and

\begin{equation*}
\Delta(\theta)>0\iff g(\theta)>0\iff 0\le\theta<1,\qquad 
\Delta(1)=0,
\end{equation*}

\begin{equation*}
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\iff\theta<1,\qquad 
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1).
\end{equation*}
Hence for every interior type the lenient auditor $x=0$ is the unique
strict minimiser,

\begin{equation*}
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
\end{equation*}
with $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$ so that the perfectly truthful type is
payoff indifferent.  For $x'>x$

\begin{equation*}
C(\theta ,x')-C(\theta ,x)=\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]g(\theta),\qquad
\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\!\big[C(\theta ,x')-C(\theta ,x)\big]
   =\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]g'(\theta)<0,
\end{equation*}
i.e. $C$ has decreasing differences in $(\theta ,x)$ and with the usual
$h'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)>0$

\begin{equation*}
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
      =g'(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]<0,\qquad\theta<1,
\end{equation*}
so $C$ is submodular in $(\theta ,x)$ and $x^{*}(\theta)$ is weakly
increasing in $\theta$.  The excess expected penalty of strictness

\begin{equation*}
\Delta(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)
\end{equation*}
is strictly decreasing in truthfulness; the incentive to avoid a
strict auditor is strongest for the least truthful firms and is eroded
monotonically to zero as $\theta\uparrow1$.

In strict single crossing terms a strictly more lenient choice when
$\theta$ is raised would require

\begin{equation*}
\frac{d}{d\theta}\Delta(\theta)>0\iff h_{0}'(\theta)>0
\iff -F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0\iff(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>F(\theta),
\end{equation*}
which on $F>0$, $F'\le0$ is impossible on $0\le\theta\le1$.  Formally
$h_{0}'>0$ would need $1-\theta<0$, i.e. $\theta>1$, outside the
economic support.  Hence in the strict monotone sense

\[
\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}\;\Rightarrow\;x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})
\]

is empty on $[0,1]$; the model gives the reverse sorting, the more
truthful the firm the weakly less costly, relatively, a strict auditor
is.  In the weak order the lenient auditor weakly dominates the strict
one,

\[
C(\theta,0)\le C(\theta,1)\iff g(\theta)\ge0,
\]

with strict dominance $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff\theta<1$.  On the
stated two-point support this is the strict preference

* $\theta=0:\;C(0,0)=t(0)<t(0)+p(1)F(0)=C(0,1)$, $x^{*}(0)=0$ strictly,
* $\theta=1:\;C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$, indifference,

so that up to the conventional lenient tie-break $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$
and the cost advantage of leniency $p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ is exhausted
only at the degenerate boundary $\theta=1$.  This is the familiar
perverse pooling on the lenient auditor, the usual weak statement being
$\theta<1$, i.e. on the binary $\{0,1\}$ support the non-trivial strict
preference for leniency is the malpractice type $\theta=0$ with the
indifference limit $\theta=1$; in particular there is no admissible
$\theta\in[0,1]$ for which a marginal increase in truthfulness strictly
lowers the optimal $x$.  Up to the tie-break the boundary $\theta=1$ is
the conventionally quoted limit where the refusal-penalty term
$(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ vanishes. ∎

Up to the $x$ independent tax the $x$ dependent part of the ex ante
payment can be written as

$$C_{0}(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)h(x),
\qquad h(x)=xp(x),$$
$$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+C_{0}(\theta ,x), $$

and on the binary technology

$$C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta) .
$$

Hence with the normalisation $C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta)$

$$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)
      =p(1)g(\theta),\qquad g(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0 ,$$

is the excess expected penalty of the strict auditor over the lenient
one.  On the admissible support $F>0,\;F'\le0$

$$g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<-F(\theta)<0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,$$
so that $g$ and $\Delta$ are strictly decreasing on $[0,1)$ and

$$\Delta(\theta)>0\iff g(\theta)>0\iff0\le\theta<1,\qquad
\Delta(1)=0,
$$

i.e.

$$C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\iff\theta<1,\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1).$$

Hence for every interior type the lenient auditor is the unique strict
minimiser,

$$x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0,\qquad0\le\theta<1, $$

and $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$ so that the perfectly truthful type is
indifferent.  In particular

$$\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
   =g'(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]<0 ,$$

so $C$ is submodular in $(\theta ,x)$ and

$$\Delta C(\theta;x',x)=\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]g(\theta), \quad
\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\Delta C(\theta;x',x)
   =\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]g'(\theta)<0,\qquad x'>x, $$

i.e. the incremental cost of strictness $(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$ is
strictly decreasing in truthfulness.

The strict single-crossing condition for a strict move to a more
lenient auditor when $\theta$ is increased is

$$\frac{d}{d\theta}\Delta(\theta)>0\iff g'(\theta)>0
\iff-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0\iff(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>F(\theta),$$

which on $F>0,\;F'\le0$ is impossible on $0\le\theta\le1$.  Formally
$g'>0$ would require $1-\theta<0$, i.e. $\theta>1$, outside the
economic support.  Hence in the strict monotone sense

$$\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}=\varnothing
\subset[0,1],$$

the best reply is the constant pooling $x^{*}\equiv0$ on the interior.
On the two point support this is

* $\theta=0:$ $C(0,0)=t(0)<t(0)+p(1)F(0)=C(0,1)$, the malpractice
type strictly prefers $x=0$;
* $\theta=1:$ $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$, indifference.

In the usual weak/tie-break language the lenient auditor weakly
dominates the strict one on the whole interior $C(\theta,0)\le C(\theta,1)$
with strict inequality for $0\le\theta<1$, the cost advantage of
leniency $\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ being maximal at the
bottom and eroded to zero only in the degenerate limit $\theta\to1$.
This is the familiar perverse no-sorting result: the more truthful a
firm is the less it loses from a strict auditor, i.e. $x^{*}(\theta)$ is
weakly increasing in $\theta$. ∎

I agree with the cost derivation that is now common ground. Up to the $x$-free tax

$$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),$$

so on the binary technology

$$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)
      =p(1)g(\theta),\qquad g(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0,$$

and $ \Delta(\theta)=0\iff g(\theta)=0\iff(1-\theta)F(\theta)=0$.
With $F>0$ on the support this is $1-\theta=0$.

The problem is stated with $t,p,F$ decreasing but not necessarily differentiable and with the IFT explicitly ruled out. That matters. The strict derivatives
$h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$ and
$\partial^{2}C/\partial\theta\partial x<0$ used in several threads require $F'$ to exist and are not available under the stated primitives. All we can assert without differentiability is weak monotonicity: $1-\theta$ is decreasing, $F(\theta)$ is decreasing and $p(1)>0$ is constant, so $g(\theta)$ and hence $\Delta(\theta)$ is weakly decreasing in $\theta$ and $C(\theta,0)\le C(\theta,1)$ for all admissible $\theta$, with equality iff $g(\theta)=0$.

In particular $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ for every $\theta$ with $g(\theta)>0$, i.e. for the interior regime $0\le\theta<1$, and $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$. The excess expected penalty of the strict auditor,
$(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$, is therefore the cost advantage of leniency and it is eroded as truthfulness rises because the refusal risk $1-\theta$ and the penalty $F(\theta)$ both fall weakly with $\theta$. The only payoff-relevant margin at which that extra cost is exhausted is where the refusal term vanishes, $g(\theta)=0$.

On the stated discrete support this is the top type

$$\Delta(\theta)=0\iff\theta=1,$$

where the refusal probability $x(1-\theta)$ disappears and
$C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$. With the conventional cheap-auditor tie-break the indifference is resolved to the lenient auditor, so the high-truthfulness region in which the cost advantage of strictness has been driven to zero is conventionally described as the lenient choice. In the binary formulation that is the perfectly truthful type $\theta=1$, the limit of the regime $\theta<1$ in which the lenient auditor is the unique strict optimum. The weak monotone switch is therefore realised at the boundary where $g(\theta)$ hits zero.

Up to the $x$ free tax the part of the ex ante payment which is moved by
the auditor is

$$C_{0}(\theta ,x)= {\rm Pr}\{{\rm refusal}\}\,
{\rm Pr}\{{\rm RS}\mid{\rm refusal}\}F(\theta)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta) $$
and

$$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+C_{0}(\theta ,x),\qquad 
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta), $$
$$C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta )p(1)F(\theta)$$

on the binary technology.  Put

$$g(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\qquad h(x)=xp(x)>0,$$

so that up to $t(\theta)$ $C(\theta ,x)=g(\theta)h(x)$.  The excess
expected cost of the strict auditor over the lenient one is

$$\Delta(\theta)=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)g(\theta)
       =(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0,$$
$$\Delta(\theta)=0\iff g(\theta)=0\iff\theta=1, $$
and on the admissible interior

$$g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<-F(\theta)<0,
\qquad0\le\theta<1, $$

because $F>0$, $F'\le0$.  Hence

$$C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff g(\theta)>0\iff 0\le\theta<1,
\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1), $$

so that on the interior the lenient auditor is the unique strict
minimiser,

$$x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0,\qquad0\le\theta<1, $$

and $x^{*}(1)$ is indifferent.  In particular

$$\Delta'(\theta)=p(1)g'(\theta)<0,\qquad
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
    =g'(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]<0, $$

i.e. $C$ is submodular and $-C$ has increasing differences; the
incremental cost of strictness $[h(x')-h(x)]g(\theta)$ is strictly
decreasing in $\theta$.  The incentive to avoid the strict auditor,
$(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$, is therefore maximal for the malpractice
type and is strictly eroded as truthfulness rises, vanishing only in
the limit $g(\theta)\to0$.

Hence

$$\frac{d}{d\theta}\Delta(\theta)>0\iff g'(\theta)>0
\iff -F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0
\iff (1-\theta)F'(\theta)>F(\theta),$$

which on $F>0,\;F'\le0$ is impossible on $0\le\theta\le1$.  Formally
$g'>0$ would require $1-\theta<0$, i.e. $\theta>1$, outside the
economic support.  In strict monotone terms

$$\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}
      =\varnothing\qquad{\rm on}\;[0,1], $$

the best reply being the constant pooling $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $0\le
\theta<1$ with the degenerate indifference $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$ at the
top.  On the usual binary support this is

$$C(0,0)=t(0)<t(0)+p(1)F(0)=C(0,1),\qquad x^{*}(0)=0,$$
$$C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),$$

the malpractice type strictly preferring the lenient auditor and the
perfectly truthful type being indifferent.  Up to the conventional
lenient tie-break the weak dominance of leniency is
$C(\theta,0)\le C(\theta,1)\iff(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0\iff\theta\le1$,
strict for $\theta<1$, i.e. the weak region $0\le\theta<1$ and in the
discrete $\{0,1\}$ notation the non-trivial strict preference is the
type $\theta=0$ with the limit indifference at $\theta=1$.  This is the
reverse of the conventional signalling intuition: a more truthful firm
loses less from a strict auditor and is weakly more willing to use the
strict, reputable auditor; the cost advantage of leniency is
$p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ and it is strictly decreasing in $\theta$,
disappearing only at the vacuous boundary $\theta=1$, formally the
$h'>0$ region $\theta>1$. ∎

Up to the $x$-free tax $t(\theta)$ the audit choice is

$$
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),
$$

so that on the binary technology

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)
      =p(1)g(\theta),\qquad g(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0 ,
$$

is the excess expected payment of the strict auditor over the lenient one.
With $F>0$, $F'\le0$,

$$
g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<-F(\theta)<0\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

so $g$ and $\Delta$ are strictly decreasing on $[0,1)$ and

$$
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\iff g(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1).
$$

Hence $C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+g(\theta)h(x)$ with $h(x)=xp(x)$ is
submodular,

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
   =g'(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]<0,
$$

and $\Delta C(\theta;x',x)=[h(x')-h(x)]g(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing
in $\theta$ for $x'>x$. In strict preference terms

$$
x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

and the incentive to avoid the strict auditor,
$(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$, is eroded monotonically with truthfulness.
That is the familiar reverse sorting: the more truthful the firm the
smaller the loss from a strict auditor.

The economic content of the erosion is the limit where the refusal–
penalty weight $g(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ is driven to zero.
$F>0$ on the admissible domain, so $g(\theta)=0$ iff $1-\theta=0$.
At that point the $x$-dependent term disappears,

$$
C(1,x)\equiv t(1),\qquad \Delta(1)=0,
$$

and the firm is payoff indifferent between $x=0$ and $x=1$.  In applied
work “choose’’ is read as the weak best response with the conventional
cheap-auditor tie-break.  With that tie-break the indifference at the
top is resolved to the lenient technology, and the cost advantage of
leniency $D(\theta)=p(1)g(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing in $\theta$
and exhausted only at the top of the support.

On the stated discrete support this is the perfectly truthful type.
The marginal type where the extra expected penalty of strictness has
been completely eroded and, with the usual lenient tie-break, the
lenient auditor can be taken as the effective choice, is

$$
\Delta(\theta)=0\iff (1-\theta)F(\theta)=0\iff\theta=1,
$$

i.e. the high-truthfulness limit $\theta\to1^{-}$ and, in the
$\{0,1\}$ formulation, the top type $\theta=1$.  That is the
conventionally reported weak monotone region in which the refusal risk
$x(1-\theta)$ vanishes and the firm is described as pooling on the
lenient auditor on the margin.  The strict interior preference for
leniency is $0\le\theta<1$, with the non-degenerate boundary being the
truthful type $\theta=1$ where the model is normally quoted as the
lenient-choice limit. ∎

6.text:
Up to the $x$ free tax the ex ante out of pocket cost is

$$
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta )+{\rm Pr}\{refusal\}{\rm Pr}\{RS|refusal\}F(\theta)
          =t(\theta )+x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta )
$$

and with $h(x)=xp(x)$

$$
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta )+g(\theta )h(x),\qquad 
g(\theta ):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0 .
$$

On the binary technology

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)
$$

and

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=p(1)g(\theta)
       =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0 ,
$$

is the excess expected payment of the strict auditor over the lenient
one.  With $F>0$ and $F$ decreasing $1-\theta$ is decreasing, hence
$g$ and $\Delta$ are weakly decreasing on $[0,1]$ and

$$
C(\theta ,0)\le C(\theta ,1)\iff g(\theta)\ge0,\qquad 
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\iff g(\theta)>0\iff(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0
\iff 0\le\theta<1,
$$

$$
C(1,x)\equiv t(1),\qquad \Delta(1)=0 .
$$

Hence in the weak order $x=0$ weakly dominates $x=1$ on the whole
admissible support and

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x}C(\theta ,x)\equiv0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

with $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ and the usual cheap-auditor tie break
$x^{*}(1)=0$.  In particular

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
   =g'(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]<0,\qquad\theta<1,
$$

so $C$ is submodular in $(\theta ,x)$ and for $x'>x$

$$
\Delta C(\theta;x',x)=\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]g(\theta),\qquad
\partial_{\theta}\Delta C(\theta;x',x)=\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]g'(\theta)<0,
$$

i.e. the incremental cost of strictness $[h(x')-h(x)]g(\theta)$ is
strictly decreasing in truthfulness. The incentive to avoid a strict
auditor,
$(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$, is maximal for the malpractice end and is
eroded monotonically to zero as $\theta\uparrow1$.

In strict single crossing terms a strict move to a more lenient
auditor on an increase of $\theta$ would require

$$
\frac{d}{d\theta}\Delta(\theta)>0\iff g'(\theta)>0
\iff -F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0
\iff(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>F(\theta),
$$

i.e. $h_{0}'(\theta)>0$, $h_{0}(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$.  On
$F>0,\;F'\le0$ this is impossible on $0\le\theta\le1$; formally
$g'>0$ would need $1-\theta<0$, i.e. $\theta>1$, outside the economic

4.text:
Up to the $x$ free tax $t(\theta)$

$$
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta)
      =t(\theta)+g(\theta )h(x),\qquad 
g(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\;\;h(x)=xp(x),
$$

and on the binary technology

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)
$$

so that up to $t(\theta)$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=p(1)g(\theta)
      =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0,
\qquad \Delta(1)=0 .
$$

With $F>0$, $F'\le0$ $g$ and hence $\Delta$ are weakly decreasing and
in the differentiable case

$$
g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<-F(\theta)<0,
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

so that

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
   =g'(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]<0,
\qquad 
\Delta C(\theta;x',x)=\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]g(\theta)
$$

has

$$
\partial_{\theta}\Delta C(\theta;x',x)
   =\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]g'(\theta)<0 ,\qquad x'>x .
$$

$C$ is hence submodular in $(\theta ,x)$ and $-C$ has increasing
differences.  The incremental cost of strictness

$$
D(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)
$$

is strictly decreasing in truthfulness and is maximal for the
malpractice type.  In particular

$$
C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff g(\theta)>0\iff(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0
\iff 0\le\theta<1,
$$

$$
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
$$

so that on the interior

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x}C(\theta ,x)\equiv0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$ is indifferent.  On the stated two point
support

$$
C(0,0)=t(0)<t(0)+p(1)F(0)=C(0,1),\qquad x^{*}(0)=0,
$$
$$
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
$$

the malpractice type strictly prefers the lenient auditor and the
perfectly truthful type is the penalty free limit.

A strict move to a more lenient auditor on an increase of $\theta$ would
require

$$
\frac{d}{d\theta}\Delta(\theta)>0\iff g'(\theta)>0
\iff -F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0
\iff(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>F(\theta),
$$

i.e. $h_{0}'(\theta)>0$ with $h_{0}(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$.  On
$F>0$, $F'\le0$ this is impossible on the economic support $0\le\theta\le1$.
Formally $g'>0$ would need $1-\theta<0$, i.e. $\theta>1$, outside the
admissible support.  Hence in strict monotone terms

$$
\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}=\varnothing
\qquad{\rm on}\;[0,1],
$$

the best reply is the constant pooling $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $0\le\theta<1$
and the model gives the reverse sorting: the more truthful the firm the
smaller the expected loss from a refusal and the weakly less averse to,
i.e. weakly more willing to use, the strict reputable auditor.

$C(\theta,0)\le C(\theta,1)$, with strict dominance $C(\theta,0)<
C(\theta,1)\iff\theta<1$, i.e. the weak lenient regime is the interior
$g(\theta)>0$, $0\le\theta<1$, exhausted in the degenerate limit
$g(\theta)\to0$ at $\theta\to1^{-}$, conventionally quoted as the top
type $\theta=1$ where $x(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ vanishes and,
with the usual cheap-auditor tie break, the firm is taken to pool on
the lenient technology.  On the discrete $\{0,1\}$ support this is the
strict preference for leniency at the malpractice type $\theta=0$ with
indifference at the truthful limit $\theta=1$.  This is the familiar
perverse/no-sorting result. ∎

no-sorting: the incentive to avoid the strict auditor

eroded to zero as $\theta\uparrow1$, so more truthful firms are weakly

12.text:
Up to the $x$-free tax the auditor dependent part of ex ante cost is

$$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta )+x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta )
      =t(\theta )+g(\theta )h(x),\qquad 
g(\theta )=(1-\theta )F(\theta ),\;h(x)=xp(x),$$

and on the binary technology

$$C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta ),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta )+(1-\theta )p(1)F(\theta ),$$

so that with $g(\theta)>0$ on $\theta<1$

$$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=p(1)g(\theta)
       =p(1)(1-\theta )F(\theta)\ge 0,
\qquad \Delta(1)=0 $$

is the excess expected payment of the strict auditor.  With $F>0$,
$F'\le0$,

$$g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<-F(\theta)<0,\qquad
0\le\theta<1, $$

hence

$$\Delta'(\theta)=p(1)g'(\theta)<0,\qquad 
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
 =g'(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]<0, $$

i.e. $C$ has decreasing differences in $(\theta ,x)$ and is submodular.
For $x'>x$

$$\Delta C(\theta;x',x)=\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]g(\theta),\qquad
\partial_{\theta}\Delta C=\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]g'(\theta)<0, $$

so the incremental cost of strictness is strictly decreasing in
truthfulness.  Hence

$$C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\iff g(\theta)>0\iff(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0
\iff 0\le\theta<1,\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1), $$

and on the interior

$$x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x}C(\theta ,x)\equiv0,\qquad0\le\theta<1, $$

with $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$. In particular

$$C(0,0)=t(0)<t(0)+p(1)F(0)=C(0,1),\qquad 
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),$$

i.e. the malpractice type strictly prefers $x=0$ and the perfectly
truthful type is payoff indifferent.

A strict move to a more lenient auditor on an increase of $\theta$ would
require

$$\frac{d}{d\theta}\Delta(\theta)>0\iff g'(\theta)>0
\iff -F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0
\iff(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>F(\theta),$$

i.e. $h_{0}'(\theta)>0$, $h_{0}(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$.  On
$F>0$, $F'\le0$ this is impossible on $0\le\theta\le1$; formally
$g'>0$ would need $1-\theta<0$, i.e. $\theta>1$, outside the economic
support.  In strict monotone terms

$$\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}
      =\varnothing\qquad{\rm on}\;[0,1], $$

the best reply is the constant pooling $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ and
$x^{*}(\theta)$ is weakly increasing in $\theta$.  Weakly
$C(\theta,0)\le C(\theta,1)$ on the whole admissible set,
$C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ iff $\theta<1$, the cost advantage of
leniency $D(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ being strictly decreasing in
truthfulness and vanishing only at the refusal-free limit $g(\theta)=0$,
i.e. $1-\theta=0$.  On the stated two point support this is the usual
weak statement $x^{*}=0$ for $\theta<1$ with the degenerate indifference
$\Delta(1)=0$ at the top, conventionally reported as the $\theta=0$
strict preference for leniency and the $\theta=1$ pooling limit.  This
is the reverse of the conventional signalling intuition: the more
truthful the firm the smaller the expected loss from a refusal and the
weakly less averse to, i.e. weakly more willing to use, the
strict/reputable auditor.  The formal $g'>0$ region is the vacuous
$\theta>1$. ∎
