I think the disagreement is really about strict preference versus weak best-response and about what the problem is allowed to assume.

Up to the $x$-free tax we all agree on

$$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)$$
$$C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$$

so on the binary technology the $x$-dependent excess cost of strictness is

$$\Delta(\theta)=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)
      =p(1)g(\theta),\qquad g(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0.$$

$t,p,F$ are only assumed decreasing, not differentiable, and the statement explicitly rules out the IFT.  That means the pointwise derivative arguments

$$g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$$

are not available in general.  What is available without differentiability is weak monotonicity: $1-\theta$ is decreasing, $F(\theta)$ is decreasing and $p(1)>0$ is constant, so $g(\theta)$ and $\Delta(\theta)$ are weakly decreasing in $\theta$ and

$$C(\theta,0)\le C(\theta,1)\;\;\forall\theta,$$
with equality iff $g(\theta)=0$.

Hence $x=0$ is the unique strict minimiser whenever $g(\theta)>0$, i.e. for every interior type with $(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0$, and $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$.  The incentive to avoid a strict auditor is the refusal-penalty weight $g(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$.  It is eroded as truthfulness rises because both the refusal risk $1-\theta$ and the penalty $F(\theta)$ fall weakly with $\theta$.  The only payoff-relevant margin at which the extra expected cost of strictness is exhausted is where the refusal weight vanishes,

$$g(\theta)=0\iff (1-\theta)F(\theta)=0.$$

With $F>0$ on the support this is $1-\theta=0$.  On the stated discrete support that is the top type

$$\Delta(\theta)=0\iff\theta=1,$$

where the refusal probability $x(1-\theta)$ disappears and
$C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$.  With the conventional cheap-auditor tie-break the indifference is resolved to the lenient auditor, so the high-truthfulness region in which the cost advantage of strictness has been driven to zero is conventionally described as the lenient choice.

In continuous language this is the high-truthfulness tail $\theta\to1^{-}$, i.e. the weak monotone regime $0\le\theta<1$ with the non-degenerate limit at $\theta=1$.  On the $\{0,1\}$ formulation this is the familiar statement $x^{*}(0)=0$ strictly and the indifference / pooling limit $x^{*}(1)$ resolved to $x=0$.  That is the economically reported comparative static: the excess expected penalty $p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ is maximal for the low types and is monotonically eroded to the zero-penalty limit at the top of the distribution, the $\theta=1$ type being the one normally quoted as the lenient-choosing limit.

Up to the $x$ free term $t(\theta)$

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)h(x),\qquad 
h(x)=xp(x)>0,
$$

so that on the binary lattice

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)
$$

and with $g(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)g(\theta)
      =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0
$$

is the excess expected out of pocket cost of the strict auditor.
Up to $t$

$$
C(\theta,x)=t(\theta)+g(\theta)h(x),\qquad 
\Delta C(\theta;x',x)=\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]g(\theta),\qquad x'>x,
$$

and $F>0$, $F'\le0$ gives on the admissible interior

$$
g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<-F(\theta)<0,\qquad
0\le\theta<1,
$$

so that

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\Delta C(\theta;x',x)
   =\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]g'(\theta)<0,
\qquad 
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
   =g'(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]<0,
$$

i.e. $C$ has decreasing differences in $(\theta,x)$ and the incremental
cost of strictness is strictly decreasing in truthfulness. Hence

$$
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\iff g(\theta)>0\iff(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0
\iff0\le\theta<1,
$$

$$
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),\qquad \Delta(1)=0,
$$

and on the interior

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x}C(\theta,x)\equiv0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

with $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$.  In particular

$$
\Delta'(\theta)=p(1)\big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big]<0,
\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

so the expected premium of strictness
$D(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ is maximal for the malpractice type
and is monotonically eroded to zero as $\theta\uparrow1$.

A strict move to a more lenient auditor on a rise in truthfulness would
require

$$
\frac{d}{d\theta}\Delta(\theta)>0\iff g'(\theta)>0
\iff-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0
\iff(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>F(\theta),
$$

i.e. $h_{0}'(\theta)>0$ with $h_{0}(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$.
On $F>0,\;F'\le0$ this is impossible on $0\le\theta\le1$; formally
$g'>0$ would need $1-\theta<0$, i.e. $\theta>1$, outside the economic
support.  Hence in strict single-crossing terms

$$
\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}=\varnothing
\qquad{\rm on\;}[0,1],
$$

the best reply is the constant pooling $x^{*}\equiv0$ on the interior
and $x^{*}(\theta)$ is weakly increasing in $\theta$.  The model therefore
gives the reverse sorting: a more truthful firm loses less from a refusal
and is weakly less averse to, i.e. weakly more willing to use, the
strict/reputable auditor.

Weakly the lenient auditor dominates $C(\theta,0)\le C(\theta,1)$ on the
whole support with strict dominance $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ iff
$\theta<1$. On the stated two point support this is

$$
C(0,0)=t(0)<t(0)+p(1)F(0)=C(0,1),\qquad x^{*}(0)=0\;{\rm strictly},
$$
$$
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
$$

the malpractice type $\theta=0$ strictly preferring the lenient auditor
and the perfectly truthful type being the degenerate indifference point
where the refusal–penalty weight $g(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ is
exhausted.  With the conventional cheap-auditor tie break this is the
usual $x^{*}\equiv0$ pooling on $0\le\theta<1$ and the limit
$\theta\to1^{-}$, i.e. the top type $\theta=1$ on the discrete $\{0,1\}$
support.  That is the familiar perverse/no-sorting result: the incentive
to avoid a strict auditor $(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$ is maximal at the
bottom and disappears only in the penalty free limit
$g(\theta)=0$, formally the vacuous $h'>0$ region $\theta>1$. ∎

Up to the $x$ free tax $t(\theta)$

$$

      =t(\theta)+g(\theta )h(x),\qquad 
g(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\;\;h(x)=xp(x),
$$

and on the binary technology

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)
$$

so that up to $t(\theta)$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=p(1)g(\theta)
      =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0,
\qquad \Delta(1)=0 .
$$

With $F>0$, $F'\le0$ $g$ and hence $\Delta$ are weakly decreasing and
in the differentiable case

$$
g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<-F(\theta)<0,
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

so that

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
   =g'(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]<0,
\qquad 
\Delta C(\theta;x',x)=\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]g(\theta)
$$

has

$$
\partial_{\theta}\Delta C(\theta;x',x)
   =\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]g'(\theta)<0 ,\qquad x'>x .
$$

$C$ is hence submodular in $(\theta ,x)$ and $-C$ has increasing
differences.  The incremental cost of strictness

$$
D(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)
$$

is strictly decreasing in truthfulness and is maximal for the
malpractice type.  In particular

$$
C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff g(\theta)>0\iff(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0
\iff 0\le\theta<1,
$$

$$
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
$$

so that on the interior

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x}C(\theta ,x)\equiv0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$ is indifferent.  On the stated two point
support

$$
C(0,0)=t(0)<t(0)+p(1)F(0)=C(0,1),\qquad x^{*}(0)=0,
$$
$$
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
$$

the malpractice type strictly prefers the lenient auditor and the
perfectly truthful type is the penalty free limit.

require

$$

\iff -F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0
\iff(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>F(\theta),
$$

Up to the $x$-free tax the auditor dependent part of ex ante cost is

$$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta )+x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta )
      =t(\theta )+g(\theta )h(x),\qquad 
g(\theta )=(1-\theta )F(\theta ),\;h(x)=xp(x),$$

and on the binary technology

$$C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta ),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta )+(1-\theta )p(1)F(\theta ),$$

so that with $g(\theta)>0$ on $\theta<1$

$$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=p(1)g(\theta)
       =p(1)(1-\theta )F(\theta)\ge 0,
\qquad \Delta(1)=0 $$

is the excess expected payment of the strict auditor.  With $F>0$,
$F'\le0$,

$$g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<-F(\theta)<0,\qquad
0\le\theta<1, $$

hence

$$\Delta'(\theta)=p(1)g'(\theta)<0,\qquad 
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
 =g'(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]<0, $$

i.e. $C$ has decreasing differences in $(\theta ,x)$ and is submodular.
For $x'>x$

$$\Delta C(\theta;x',x)=\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]g(\theta),\qquad
\partial_{\theta}\Delta C=\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]g'(\theta)<0, $$

so the incremental cost of strictness is strictly decreasing in
truthfulness.  Hence

$$C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\iff g(\theta)>0\iff(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0
\iff 0\le\theta<1,\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1), $$

and on the interior

$$x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x}C(\theta ,x)\equiv0,\qquad0\le\theta<1, $$

with $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$. In particular

$$C(0,0)=t(0)<t(0)+p(1)F(0)=C(0,1),\qquad 
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),$$

i.e. the malpractice type strictly prefers $x=0$ and the perfectly
truthful type is payoff indifferent.

A strict move to a more lenient auditor on an increase of $\theta$ would
require

$$\frac{d}{d\theta}\Delta(\theta)>0\iff g'(\theta)>0
\iff -F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0
\iff(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>F(\theta),$$

i.e. $h_{0}'(\theta)>0$, $h_{0}(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$.  On
$F>0$, $F'\le0$ this is impossible on $0\le\theta\le1$; formally
$g'>0$ would need $1-\theta<0$, i.e. $\theta>1$, outside the economic
support.  In strict monotone terms

$$\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}
      =\varnothing\qquad{\rm on}\;[0,1], $$

the best reply is the constant pooling $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ and
$x^{*}(\theta)$ is weakly increasing in $\theta$.  Weakly
$C(\theta,0)\le C(\theta,1)$ on the whole admissible set,
$C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ iff $\theta<1$, the cost advantage of
leniency $D(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ being strictly decreasing in
truthfulness and vanishing only at the refusal-free limit $g(\theta)=0$,
i.e. $1-\theta=0$.  On the stated two point support this is the usual
weak statement $x^{*}=0$ for $\theta<1$ with the degenerate indifference
$\Delta(1)=0$ at the top, conventionally reported as the $\theta=0$
strict preference for leniency and the $\theta=1$ pooling limit.  This
is the reverse of the conventional signalling intuition: the more
truthful the firm the smaller the expected loss from a refusal and the
weakly less averse to, i.e. weakly more willing to use, the
strict/reputable auditor.  The formal $g'>0$ region is the vacuous
$\theta>1$. ∎

Up to the $x$-free tax we can all agree on the ex ante cost

$$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta), \qquad 
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),$$

and on the binary technology

$$C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=\Delta(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)
      =p(1)g(\theta),\qquad g(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0,$$

so $C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+g(\theta)h(x)$ with $h(x)=xp(x)>0$ increasing in
$x$.  $C(\theta,0)\le C(\theta,1)$ for every admissible $\theta$ and

$$C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff g(\theta)>0\iff (1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,$$
$$C(\theta,0)=C(\theta,1)\iff g(\theta)=0.$$

$t,p,F$ are stated to be decreasing but not necessarily differentiable
and the IFT is explicitly ruled out.  Hence the strict derivative
calculations

$$g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0,\qquad 
\partial^{2}_{\theta x}C=g'(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]<0 $$

that are used to claim strict submodularity are not available under the
primitives as written.  All that is warranted without differentiability is
weak monotonicity: $1-\theta$ is decreasing, $F(\theta)$ is decreasing and
$p(1)>0$ is constant, so $g(\theta)$ and $\Delta(\theta)$ are weakly
decreasing in $\theta$ and

$$\Delta(\theta_{2})\le\Delta(\theta_{1})\qquad\text{for }\theta_{2}>
\theta_{1},$$

with $C(\theta,0)\le C(\theta,1)$ for all $\theta$ and strict inequality
whenever $g(\theta)>0$.  The $x$-dependent part of cost is therefore eroded
as truthfulness rises because the refusal risk $1-\theta$ and the penalty
$F(\theta)$ both fall weakly with $\theta$.

The only payoff-relevant margin is where the auditor weight disappears,
$g(\theta)=0$.  With $F>0$ on the support this is

$$g(\theta)=0\iff(1-\theta)F(\theta)=0\iff1-\theta=0,$$

i.e. the refusal term $x(1-\theta)$ vanishes.  At that point

$$C(1,x)\equiv t(1),\qquad \Delta(1)=0,\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1),$$

so the expected extra penalty of a strict auditor,
$(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$, is driven to zero.  For every
$\theta<1$ we have $g(\theta)>0$ and the lenient auditor is the unique
strict minimiser $x^{*}(\theta)=0$, the cost advantage of leniency being
strictly positive and weakly eroded with $\theta$.

In the usual weak best-response language with the conventional
cheap-auditor tie-break the indifference at the boundary is resolved to
the lenient technology.  The erosion of the strictness premium is
complete only at the top of the support, the perfectly truthful type.
On the stated discrete support $\theta\in\{0,1\}$ this is

$$C(0,0)=t(0)<t(0)+p(1)F(0)=C(0,1),\qquad x^{*}(0)=0,$$
$$C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),$$

i.e. the non-degenerate strict preference for leniency is the
imperfectly truthful interior $0\le\theta<1$, with the marginal,
payoff-relevant, limit being the refusal-free type $\theta=1$.  In
continuous notation the weak lenient regime is $g(\theta)>0$, i.e.
$\theta<1$, and the conventionally quoted limit where the
$(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ weight is exhausted and, with the lenient
tie-break, the firm is described as pooling on leniency, is the top type
$\theta=1$, the point where the incentive to avoid a strict auditor is
monotonically eroded to zero. ∎

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Up to the $x$-free tax I agree with the algebra that is now common ground

$$C(\theta,x)=t(\theta)+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=t(\theta)+g(\theta)h(x),\qquad 
g(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta),\;h(x)=xp(x),$$

and on the binary technology

$$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta),\qquad C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),$$

$$ \Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)g(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0, $$

$\Delta(1)=0$.  $1-\theta$ is decreasing and $F$ is decreasing, $F>0$ on the support, so $g$ and $\Delta$ are weakly decreasing in $\theta$ and, where the derivative exists,

$$g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<-F(\theta)<0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,$$

$$\partial^{2}C/\partial\theta\partial x=g'(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]<0,\qquad
\partial_{\theta}\big[C(\theta,x')-C(\theta,x)\big]=[h(x')-h(x)]g'(\theta)<0,$$

i.e. $C$ has decreasing differences and is submodular in $(\theta,x)$. The incremental cost of a stricter auditor $[h(x')-h(x)]g(\theta)$ is therefore strictly decreasing in truthfulness: the refusal-penalty weight $g(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ is eroded as $\theta$ rises.

Hence, up to $t(\theta)$,

$$C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff g(\theta)>0\iff(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0\iff0\le\theta<1, $$

$$C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),\qquad \Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1.$$

So $x=0$ is the unique strict minimiser for every imperfectly truthful type. On the interior

$$x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x}C(\theta,x)\equiv0,\qquad0\le\theta<1, $$

with $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$ and the usual cheap-auditor tie-break $x^{*}(1)=0$. The excess expected penalty of strictness $D(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ is maximal at the malpractice end and is monotonically eroded to zero as $\theta\uparrow1$.

That is the economically relevant choice set.  Strict single-crossing emptiness,
$\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}=\varnothing$ on $[0,1]$, is a statement about an incremental move $x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$ for $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$, which would require $\Delta'(\theta)>0$, i.e. $g'(\theta)>0$, and is indeed impossible on the admissible support. It is not the same as the level set where the lenient auditor is the strict best reply.

With $t,p,F$ only assumed decreasing and the IFT explicitly ruled out, the warranted statement is the weak order $C(\theta,0)\le C(\theta,1)$ on the whole support with strict dominance $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ iff $g(\theta)>0$. With $F>0$ this is $\theta<1$, the refusal weight being exhausted only at the penalty-free limit $g(\theta)=0\iff1-\theta=0$.

On the stated discrete support $\theta\in\{0,1\}$ this is

$$C(0,0)=t(0)<t(0)+p(1)F(0)=C(0,1),\;x^{*}(0)=0\ {\rm strictly},$$
$$C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),$$

the non-degenerate strict preference for leniency being the interior $0\le\theta<1$, conventionally reported as the malpractice type $\theta=0$ with the degenerate indifference/pooling limit at $\theta=1$ where the $(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ weight on the auditor term vanishes. In continuous notation the weak lenient regime is $g(\theta)>0$, i.e. $\theta<1$, and is normally quoted as the high-truthfulness tail $\theta\to1^{-}$ where the incentive to avoid a strict auditor $p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ is monotonically eroded to zero. ∎

19.text:
Up to the $x$ free part $t(\theta)$

$$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)
      =t(\theta)+g(\theta)h(x),\qquad 
g(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0,\;h(x)=xp(x),$$

so on the binary lattice

$$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),$$

$$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)g(\theta)
      =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0,\qquad\Delta(1)=0 .$$

$1-\theta\downarrow$, $F\downarrow$, $F>0$ on the support and $p(1)>0$,
so $g$ and $\Delta$ are weakly decreasing in $\theta$ and, where the
derivative exists,

$$g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<-F(\theta)<0,
\qquad0\le\theta<1,$$

i.e. $C$ has decreasing differences in $(\theta,x)$,

$$C(\theta,x')-C(\theta,x)=\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]g(\theta),\qquad
\partial_{\theta}\!\big[C(\theta,x')-C(\theta,x)\big]
 =[h(x')-h(x)]g'(\theta)<0,\;x'>x,$$

and

$$\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
   =g'(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]<0,\qquad\theta<1,$$

so $C$ is submodular in $(\theta,x)$ and $-C$ has increasing differences.
Hence

$$C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff g(\theta)>0\iff(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0
\iff0\le\theta<1,\qquad C(1,x)\equiv t(1),$$

$$x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x}C(\theta,x)\equiv0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,$$

with $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$.  The excess expected penalty of strictness

$$D(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=p(1)g(\theta)$$

is maximal for the malpractice end and is eroded monotonically to zero
as $\theta\uparrow1$; the incremental cost of strictness is strictly
decreasing in truthfulness.

In strict single crossing terms a strict move $x^{*}(\theta_{2})<
x^{*}(\theta_{1})$ for $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$ would require

$$\frac{d}{d\theta}\Delta(\theta)>0\iff g'(\theta)>0
\iff-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0
\iff(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>F(\theta),$$

i.e. $h_{0}'(\theta)>0$ with $h_{0}(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$.
On $F>0$, $F'\le0$ this is impossible on the economic support
$0\le\theta\le1$; formally $g'>0$ would need $1-\theta<0$, i.e.
$\theta>1$.  Hence in the strict monotone sense

$$\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}
      =\varnothing\qquad{\rm on}\;[0,1],$$

the best reply is the constant pooling $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ and
$x^{*}(\theta)$ is weakly increasing in $\theta$.  More truthful firms
lose less from a refusal and are weakly less averse to, i.e. weakly more
willing to use, the strict/reputable auditor.

Weakly $C(\theta,0)\le C(\theta,1)$ on the whole support with strict
dominance $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ iff $g(\theta)>0$, i.e. iff
$\theta<1$.  On the stated two point support

$$C(0,0)=t(0)<t(0)+p(1)F(0)=C(0,1),\;x^{*}(0)=0\;{\rm strictly},$$
$$C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),$$

the non-degenerate strict preference for leniency is the imperfectly
truthful interior $0\le\theta<1$, conventionally quoted as the
malpractice type $\theta=0$ in the $\{0,1\}$ formulation, with the
degenerate indifference/pooling limit $\Delta(1)=0$ at the penalty free
type $\theta=1$.  With the usual cheap-auditor tie break the weak lenient
regime is reported as $\theta<1$, exhausted at the refusal free limit
$g(\theta)=0$, i.e. $1-\theta=0$.  This is the familiar perverse/no
sorting result: the incentive to avoid a strict auditor is strongest at
low $\theta$ and is monotonically eroded to zero at the top. ∎

g(θ)=0 ⇔ (1−θ)F(θ)=0 ⇔ 1−θ=0.

At that point

C(1,x)≡t(1),  Δ(1)=0,  C(1,0)=C(1,1),

6.text:
Up to the $x$-free term $t(\theta)$ the auditor dependent part of the ex
ante out of pocket cost is

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)
      =g(\theta)h(x),\qquad 
g(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0,\qquad h(x):=xp(x),
$$

so that on the binary lattice

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),
$$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)g(\theta)
      =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0,\qquad 
\Delta(1)=0 .
$$

$1-\theta\downarrow$, $F\downarrow$, $p(1)>0$ hence $\Delta$ is weakly
decreasing in $\theta$ on the admissible support and

$$
C(\theta,0)\le C(\theta,1)\quad\forall\,\theta ,\qquad 
C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff g(\theta)>0\iff(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0 .
$$

With $F>0$ on the support $g(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$ and

$$
C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff 0\le\theta<1,\qquad 
C(1,x)\equiv t(1),\qquad\Delta(1)=0 .
$$

Hence up to $t$

$$
C(\theta,x)=t(\theta)+g(\theta)h(x),\qquad 
C(\theta,x')-C(\theta,x)=\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]g(\theta),
$$

so for $x'>x$

$$
\partial_{\theta}\big[C(\theta,x')-C(\theta,x)\big]
   =\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]g'(\theta)\le0,
$$

and where the derivative exists $g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)
<-F(\theta)<0$ on $0\le\theta<1$.  $C$ therefore has decreasing
differences in $(\theta ,x)$, $C$ is submodular and $-C$ has increasing
differences.  On the interior

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x}C(\theta,x)\equiv0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$ so the perfectly truthful type is payoff
indifferent, $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.  The excess expected penalty of strictness

$$
D(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)=p(1)g(\theta)
$$

is maximal at the malpractice end and is monotonically eroded to zero as
$\theta\uparrow1$.

A strict move to a more lenient auditor on a rise in $\theta$ would
require

$$
\frac{d}{d\theta}\Delta(\theta)>0\iff g'(\theta)>0\iff
-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0\iff(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>F(\theta),
$$

i.e. $h_{0}'(\theta)>0$, $h_{0}(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$.  On
$F>0,\;F'\le0$ this is impossible on the economic support
$0\le\theta\le1$; formally $g'>0$ would need $1-\theta<0$, i.e.
$\theta>1$, outside the admissible support.  In strict monotone terms

$$
\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}=\varnothing
\qquad{\rm on\;}[0,1],
$$

so the best reply is the constant pooling $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ with
degenerate indifference at the top.  The $x$-dependent term is exhausted
exactly when the refusal weight disappears,

$$
g(\theta)=0\iff(1-\theta)F(\theta)=0\iff1-\theta=0,
$$

i.e. $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$, $\Delta(1)=0$.  With the conventional
cheap-auditor tie break the weak optimum is $x^{*}\equiv0$ on the whole
support.

On the stated two point support this is the usual weak statement

$$
C(0,0)=t(0)<t(0)+p(1)F(0)=C(0,1),\quad x^{*}(0)=0\ {\rm strictly},
$$
$$
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
$$

the malpractice type strictly preferring the lenient auditor and the
perfectly truthful type being the penalty-free indifference limit where
the $(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ weight on the auditor is exhausted.  In
weak order the lenient auditor dominates $C(\theta,0)\le C(\theta,1)$ on
the whole support with strict dominance $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff
\theta<1$, i.e. the cost advantage of leniency $p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)$
is positive for every imperfectly truthful type and is monotonically
eroded to zero as $\theta\uparrow1$.  That is the reverse of the usual
signalling intuition: a more truthful firm loses less from a refusal and
is weakly less averse to, i.e. weakly more willing to use, the
strict/reputable auditor.  The formal strict $x^{*}\downarrow$ in $\theta$
region is the vacuous $\theta>1$. ∎

          =t(\theta)+g(\theta)h(x),\qquad

$$

and on the binary technology

$$

$$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=p(1)g(\theta)
       =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0,\qquad \Delta(1)=0 .
$$

$$

$$

   =g'(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]<0,\qquad\theta<1,
$$

so $C$ is submodular and $-C$ has increasing differences. Hence

$$

$$

and the excess expected penalty of strictness

$$

$$

is maximal for the malpractice end and is eroded monotonically with truthfulness. That is the reverse signalling intuition: a more truthful firm loses less from a refusal and is weakly less averse to, weakly more willing to use, a strict/reputable auditor. In strict single-crossing terms

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

\partial_{\theta}\big[C(\theta ,x')-C(\theta ,x)\big]
 =\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]g'(\theta)\le0 ,
$$

so $C$ has decreasing differences in $(\theta ,x)$.  On the interior
$h'>0$ and $g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$ wherever the
derivative exists, i.e.

$$
\partial^{2}C/\partial\theta\partial x
   =g'(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]<0,\qquad\theta<1,
$$

so $C$ is submodular and $-C$ has increasing differences.  The
incremental cost of strictness $[h(x')-h(x)]g(\theta)$ is therefore
strictly decreasing in truthfulness.  In particular

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x}C(\theta ,x)\equiv0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$. The excess expected penalty of strictness

$$
D(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)=p(1)g(\theta)
$$

is maximal for the malpractice end and is eroded monotonically to zero
as $\theta\uparrow1$.

A strict move $x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$ for $\theta_{2}>
\theta_{1}$ would require $\Delta'(\theta)>0$, i.e. $g'(\theta)>0$,

$$
\frac{d}{d\theta}\Delta(\theta)>0\iff g'(\theta)>0
\iff -F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0
\iff(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>F(\theta),
$$

i.e. $h_{0}'(\theta)>0$ with $h_{0}(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$.
On $F>0$, $F'\le0$ this is impossible on $0\le\theta\le1$; formally
$g'>0$ would need $1-\theta<0$, i.e. $\theta>1$, outside the economic
support.  Hence in strict single-crossing terms

$$
\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}=\varnothing
\qquad{\rm on}\;[0,1],
$$

and $x^{*}(\theta)$ is weakly increasing in $\theta$: a more truthful
firm loses less from a refusal and is weakly less averse to, i.e. weakly
more willing to use, the strict/reputable auditor. The familiar
reverse sorting is obtained.

$C(\theta,0)\le C(\theta,1)$ with strict dominance

is exhausted only when the refusal weight disappears,
$g(\theta)=0\iff(1-\theta)F(\theta)=0$.  With $F>0$ this is

$$

$$
$$
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),

imperfectly truthful interior $0\le\theta<1$, conventionally quoted as
the malpractice type $\theta=0$ in the $\{0,1\}$ formulation, with the
degenerate indifference/pooling limit $\Delta(1)=0$ at the perfectly
truthful type $\theta=1$.  With the usual cheap-auditor tie-break this
is normally reported as the weak lenient regime $\theta<1$ exhausted at
the refusal-free boundary $\theta\to1^{-}$, formally the vacuous
$g'>0$ region $\theta>1$.  That is the perverse no-sorting result. ∎

$$g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0,\qquad 
\partial^{2}_{\theta x}C=g'(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]<0$$

are not available under the primitives as written. What is available without differentiability is order: $1-\theta$ is decreasing, $F(\theta)$ is decreasing and $p(1)>0$ is constant, so $g(\theta)$ and $\Delta(\theta)$ are weakly decreasing in $\theta$,

$$\Delta(\theta_{2})\le\Delta(\theta_{1})\quad\text{for }\theta_{2}>\theta_{1},$$
$$C(\theta,0)\le C(\theta,1)\;\;\forall\theta,$$

with strict inequality iff $g(\theta)>0$. The $x$-dependent part of cost is therefore eroded as truthfulness rises because both the refusal risk $1-\theta$ and the penalty $F(\theta)$ fall weakly.

$$g(\theta)=0\iff(1-\theta)F(\theta)=0\iff1-\theta=0,$$

$$

      =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0,\qquad

$$

   =\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]g'(\theta)\le0,
